FTMO Instant Account Review — No Challenge, But Is It Really a Better Deal? 🤓

FTMO just introduced its Instant Account, and at first glance, it looks pretty attractive.

No evaluation. No profit target to pass before getting access. Pay a one-time fee, start trading immediately, and keep 90% of eligible profits.

Sounds great, right?

Well, I wouldn't pull out my credit card just yet.

The real question isn't how quickly you can get funded. It's how difficult it will be to actually get paid.

Let's look at what you're really buying.

FTMO offers five account sizes, ranging from $5,000 to $100,000, with one-time fees starting at €169 and going all the way up to €2,999.

Every account comes with a 10% maximum loss limit, a 3% daily loss limit, a 30% consistency requirement, leverage up to 1:100, and a 90% reward split.

On paper, these numbers don't look terrible.

And to give FTMO credit, there are some genuine advantages here.

You skip the evaluation process entirely. There's no pressure to hit an arbitrary profit target before you can start earning rewards, and there's no fixed trading deadline.

For an experienced trader with a proven strategy, that convenience has value.

But here's where things get less attractive.

The first problem is the trailing drawdown.

FTMO advertises a 10% maximum loss allowance. What matters, however, is that this limit trails your highest closed-trade account balance in real time.

Let's say you buy a $10,000 account.

Your initial maximum loss threshold is $9,000.

You make $800, bringing your balance to $10,800.

Great. Except your maximum loss threshold has now moved up to $9,800.

If the market turns against you, that threshold doesn't simply move back down.

And unlike a fixed drawdown model, you can't assume that your original $1,000 risk cushion will remain available forever.

For traders who like to let profits run, experience meaningful equity swings, or trade volatile instruments, this is something to take seriously.

The second problem, and probably the most frustrating one, is the 30% consistency rule.

This is where the Instant Account starts looking a lot less instant.

Imagine you have an excellent trading day and make $600.

That's a solid result.

But under the consistency rule, your best trading day cannot represent more than 30% of your total accumulated net profit.

That means you'd need at least $2,000 in total net profit before that $600 day falls within the limit, assuming no future day produces an even larger profit.

Think about that.

You made money. You followed your strategy. You didn't necessarily violate any risk limits.

Yet you're still not eligible for a reward until your profit distribution satisfies the rule.

And if you take losses along the way, reaching that required total becomes harder.

To be fair, failing the consistency requirement doesn't automatically terminate your account. You're allowed to continue trading.

But that's exactly my criticism.

A trader who has already made money may have to keep exposing that money to market risk just to qualify for a payout.

I understand why FTMO wants to encourage consistency. A firm has every reason to prefer traders who can produce repeatable results instead of relying on one lucky session.

But markets don't distribute opportunities evenly.

Some weeks offer outstanding setups. Others offer absolutely nothing.

A disciplined trader might make most of their monthly profits in two or three strong sessions and spend the remaining days protecting capital.

That doesn't automatically make the strategy inconsistent or irresponsible.

In fact, knowing when not to trade is part of being a good trader.

Yet this rule can create an uncomfortable incentive to keep trading when the better decision might be to stop.

The third issue is pricing.

€339 for a $10,000 account or €1,499 for a $50,000 account isn't exactly pocket change.

Remember, you're paying a non-refundable fee for access to a simulated trading account under a specific set of rules.

You're not purchasing $50,000 of cash, and you don't own the advertised account balance.

What you're buying is an opportunity to earn performance-based rewards.

There's nothing inherently wrong with that business model. But traders should understand the distinction before spending their money.

So who is this account actually for?

I'd say FTMO Instant makes the most sense for experienced traders who already have a tested strategy, can manage tight daily risk limits, and generate relatively steady profits across multiple sessions.

Traders who prioritize consistent execution over occasional large wins may find the structure manageable.

On the other hand, I would be much more cautious if you're a breakout trader, a swing trader whose profits arrive in bursts, or someone who depends on a few high-conviction trades to generate most of their returns.

And if you're still struggling with risk management, paying extra to skip an evaluation doesn't solve that problem.

It just makes the consequences more expensive.

My Verdict

I like the idea of removing the evaluation process.

I like the 90% reward split.

And FTMO has an established name in the prop trading industry, which certainly matters.

But I don't particularly like the combination of a relatively expensive entry fee, a trailing drawdown, and a strict 30% consistency requirement.

Individually, each rule can be justified.

Together, they make the product considerably less flexible than the marketing might suggest.

For me, the biggest weakness isn't the maximum loss limit or even the price.

It's the possibility of being profitable but still having to trade more before you're allowed to get paid.

That's a meaningful trade-off, and one that deserves more attention than the words "Instant Funding."

I wouldn't call FTMO Instant a bad product. I just wouldn't call it an obvious bargain either.

Skipping the challenge is convenient.

But convenience doesn't necessarily mean better trading conditions.

A funded account isn't valuable because of the number printed on the dashboard. It's valuable because of how realistically you can manage risk, protect profits, and withdraw money.

And that's where I think FTMO Instant still has something to prove.

Would you rather pay more to skip the challenge, or take an evaluation with fewer restrictions on how you generate your profits?
